context_blurb:
Pour a bag of trail mix into a bowl. The nuts, raisins and chocolate drops get jumbled together, yet each piece is still itself, and you could pick them apart by hand. That is a mixture. Beach sand, muddy water and the salty sea are mixtures too, and each one can be taken apart again.

In a mixture nothing new is made, so each substance keeps its own properties. Iron filings stirred into pale sand are still iron. Pass a magnet over the dish, and the iron filings jump up and cling to it, while the sand stays put. Pale sand is mostly quartz, a mineral that magnets do not pull.

A sieve is a screen full of holes: grains smaller than the holes fall through, and bigger ones stay behind. So a sieve sorts grains by their size alone. A small grain drops through, heavy or light. Geologists, who study rocks, shake sand through a stack of sieves with the biggest holes on top, so each sieve lower down holds finer sand.

Some bits are too small for any sieve. Stir sand and a pinch of salt into water, and the salt dissolves, breaking into bits far too small to see. Pour it through filter paper in a funnel, and the salt bits slip through the paper's tiny holes with the water. The sand grains are too big, so only the sand is caught on the paper. To get the salt back, let the water dry away.

Salt water is a solution: a mixture that is the same all the way through. Its dissolved bits spread evenly and are too small ever to settle. Copper sulfate, a poisonous lab chemical, has bright blue crystals that dissolve and turn water blue. Seal some in a flask for a month, and the colour never sinks. A drop from the top and a drop from the bottom are the same shade of blue, because a solution is the same in every part. Sand stirred into water is different: its grains sink to the bottom.

Salt water also freezes differently. Pure water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, but salt water must get colder first, and the saltier it is, the colder it must get. Water that is 8 percent salt freezes only at about minus 5 degrees. So road crews scatter rock salt on icy roads. It dissolves into the wet film on the ice, the salt water it makes stays liquid, and the ice it touches melts into slush. Salt lowers the temperature water freezes at; it does not heat the ice.

Does dissolved salt really vanish? A balance can tell. Weigh the water, the salt and its dish together, then stir the salt in until it can't be seen and weigh everything again. The balance shows the same mass as before, because the salt is still in the water in bits too small to see, and those bits still have mass. So 150 grams of water and 10 grams of salt make 160 grams of salt water.

Freezing keeps mass too. Cap a bottle of water, mark the water line, weigh it and freeze it overnight. The ice weighs just what the water did, but it stands above the mark. Water swells by about 9 percent as it freezes, so its volume, the space it takes up, grows while its mass stays the same. That is why ice floats: it takes up more room for its mass than water does.

Some changes do make something new. An iron nail left out in the rain for a few weeks grows a crust of reddish-brown rust. That rust is a new substance made from the iron. The iron has joined with oxygen from the air, helped by water, and rust is crumbly and weak because it is not iron any more. Rust is not just iron with a new colour, and no drying or picking apart turns it back into iron.
